questions.evidence_quote:
When ∆D = 0 (∆D ≡ |D1 − D2|), the 
inversion symmetry is preserved, and the photonic 
crystal hosts nodal lines along Wα± -X (α = x, y, z), 
forming intersecting nodal chains. The momentum of 
the six valleys are (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and 
(2π/a, 0, ±π/a) for Wx±, Wy±, and Wz±, respectively (Fig. 
1(c)). When ∆D ≠ 0, however, the inversion symmetry 
is broken, and the nodal line degeneracies are gapped 
out to form a complete photonic bandgap.

questions.question: In the Wy experiment at 13.8 GHz, which source phase winding selects Wy− and what direction is measured?

options.A: Equal phases select Wy− and outcouple at 0°
options.B: (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) selects Wy− and outcouples at −32.9°
options.C: (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2) selects Wy− and outcouples at +32.9°
options.D: (0, π, 0, π) selects Wy− and outcouples at −90°

questions.rationale: The clockwise winding is assigned to Wy−, whose measured direction is the negative angle; the opposite winding selects Wy+.
questions.evidence_quote:
Taking valley states at Wy± as an example, the 
relative phase delay of each source is set to (0, π/2, π, 
3π/2) for Wy− and (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2) for Wy+, to form 
a clockwise or counterclockwise phase winding in the 
x-z plane (see Fig. 2(a)). The excited valley states will 
outcouple to the free space radiation and, thus, the 
momentum of the excited valley state can be judged 
from the outcoupling direction (see Figs. 2(b) and (c)). 
As shown in Fig. 2(d), the measured outcoupling fields 
at 13.8 GHz exhibit different directions: for the 
clockwise (counterclockwise) phase winding, the 
direction is −32.9° (+32.9°), corresponding to Wy− 
(Wy+) , while for the case without phase winding, the 
direction is 0°, corresponding to X, since the states at X 
coexist with valley states at the same frequency [22].

questions.question: What physical feature explains the reported diffractionless propagation of the surface state?

options.A: The measured state repeatedly scatters between opposite valleys
options.B: Its flat isofrequency contour preserves group velocity as transverse wavevector varies
options.C: A quadratic dispersion makes the group velocity vanish at all transverse momenta
options.D: A large density of bulk states traps the wave at the surface

questions.rationale: The paper attributes canalization to flat contours and notes that the dispersion is independent of the wavevector transverse to propagation.
questions.evidence_quote:
Note that the chiral surface 
states exhibit canalization behaviour; that is, the surface 
states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction, 
corresponding to the Wx− valley. This canalization 
phenomenon is due to the flat isofrequancy contour of 
the surface states, which has been confirmed both 
experimentally and numerically (Fig. 3(h)) [25–27]. 
The canalization has previously been explored at the 
topological transition point between open hyperbolic 
and closed elliptical isofrequency contours, as in the 
twisted van der Waals bilayers [26]. From the equation 
of the surface states aforementioned, one can see that 
the surface dispersion is independent of the wavevector 
vertical to the propagation direction (denoted as kx (ky)), 
indicating that the group velocity of surface states 
preserves for different ky (kx) around each valley, which 
leads to the flat isofrequency contours.
questions.formatted_question:
What physical feature explains the reported diffractionless propagation of the surface state?
A) The measured state repeatedly scatters between opposite valleys

D) A large density of bulk states traps the wave at the surface

The large kernel depthwise convo-
lutions provide a large receptive field to capture long-range
low-frequency features, while Simple Gate and HardSwish are
designed with lightweight considerations.
The input x is normalized and then divided into two
branches.
Channel Attention (CA) The first branch is Channel At-
tention (CA) [15], which reallocates weights to each channel,
allowing the module to focus more on important channels
while suppressing less significant ones, resulting in a more
precise feature representation [19].
Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG) The LSG shown in Fig.
2 is responsible for establishing local spatial perspectives,
consists of depth-wise convolution, point-wise convolution,
and Learnable-Sigmoid activation function. This branch is
inspired by the Learnable-Sigmoid activation function used
in MP-SENet [5] for generating masks. Its flexibility makes it
crucial for generating accurate masks. This branch focuses on
modeling local information within the feature map, enhancing
high-frequency details and spatial invariance in the spectrum.

questions.question: Why did the authors select EY@CTAB rather than EY@TX-100 for the subsequent photocatalysis?

options.A: EY binds electrostatically to positively charged CTAB, and EY@TX-100 disassembles in K3PO4
options.B: TX-100 produced the largest lifetime increase and resisted disassembly
options.C: SDS enhanced EY fluorescence more than CTAB and remained stable in base
options.D: CTAB prevented EY association, while TX-100 concentrated the amine substrate

questions.rationale: EY is dianionic at pH 7, shows CTAB-specific spectral/lifetime evidence of association, and the TX-100 composite is unstable in base.
questions.evidence_quote: These findings suggest a higher binding affinity of EY towards CTAB (EY@CTAB) than TX-100 (EY@TX-100). This is expected as EY bears two negative charges at pH 7 32 and hence, interacts electrostatically with the positively charged CTAB. At the premicellar concentration of CTAB, EY undergoes CTAB-induced aggregation due to ion-pair formation; however, these aggregates subsequently dissociate at or near the CMC of CTAB due to entrapment of EY at the micellar Stern layer (Figure 1c ). 33, 34 This argument gains further support from the enhanced fluorescence lifetime of EY from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon micellization of CTAB (Figure 1d and Table S2 ), signifying micellar association. As the present POC reaction occurs in the presence of a base, we checked the stabilities of the micellar composites of EY in the presence of K3PO4. Although EY@CTAB is found to be stable in the presence of K3PO4, EY@TX-100 suffers disassembly (Figure S2 and S3 ). Therefore, we utilized the EY@CTAB composite for our subsequent studies.

options.A: The lifetime remains unchanged, indicating only ground-state proton transfer
options.B: A kq of 6.3×10^12 M−1s−1 and 0.3-ps PET support non-diffusive interfacial electron transfer
options.C: The lack of a linear Stern–Volmer plot rules out PET
options.D: A kq below 10^6 M−1s−1 indicates diffusion-limited transfer over seconds

questions.rationale: Both the unusually fast quenching rate and ultrafast up-conversion time constant are presented as evidence for non-diffusive PET.
questions.evidence_quote:
A linear Stern-Volmer (SV) plot with a quenching rate constant (kq) of 6.3 × 10 12 M -1 s -1 suggests a non-diffusive bimolecular quenching process (Figure 2b ). 37, 38 Quenching parameters for other arylamines are tabulated in Table S3 . Notably, lack of fluorescence quenching with p-nitroaniline suggests lack of any electron transfer to EY*@CTAB (Figure 2b ). It is noteworthy to mention that the presence of K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on the SV plots and quenching rate constant (Figure S14 ), signifying that PET precedes the proton abstraction step by base. (Figure 2c and Table S4 ). Although PET at the micellar surface is instantaneous in nature and occurs in a few picoseconds, [39] [40] [41] [42] the marked decrease in the fluorescence lifetime of EY@CTAB authenticates the excited state quenching by p-anisidine.
Fluorescence up-conversion measurements reveal an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps in the presence of p-anisidine (Figure 2d ).

questions.question: What assumptions produced the modeled 1.15-copy, 95%-probability LOD for the first primer pool?

options.A: 172 primer pairs averaging 99 bp, 6% single-strand cDNA amplification efficiency, and 80% target success
options.B: 28 targets at 99% efficiency and no failed amplicons
options.C: One RT-PCR amplicon at 6% efficiency with 50% genome recovery
options.D: 171 primer pairs averaging 158 bp, 26% efficiency, and 100% target success

questions.rationale: The model combines the 172-pair panel design with conservative amplification and target-recovery assumptions.
questions.evidence_quote: We designed a panel of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers in order to increase the sensitivity of detecting SARS-CoV-2 (Fig. 1B ). The average amplicon length is 99bp. The amplicons span across the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome with an average 76bp gap (76±10bp) between adjacent amplicons. Since the observed efficiency of multiplex PCR is about 26% in amplifying the four DNA strands of a pair of human chromosomes, we assumed an efficiency of 6% in amplifying the single-strand of a cDNA molecule. In addition, it has already been reported that 79% of variants are recovered when directly amplifying 600 amplicons from a single cell using our technology 37 . Therefore, we assumed that 80% of targeted regions would be amplified successfully. Using the same mathematical model described above, we estimated that our SARS-CoV-2 panel can detect 1.15 copies of the virus at 95% probability

What assumptions produced the modeled 1.15-copy, 95%-probability LOD for the first primer pool?

C) One RT-PCR amplicon at 6% efficiency with 50% genome recovery

options.C: It increased the first pool from 172 to 343 pairs without overlap
options.D: It amplified only the S gene, eliminating the N-gene targets

questions.rationale: The second pool was deliberately complementary to first-pool gaps, increasing the chance of at least one target occurrence.
questions.evidence_quote: We also designed a second pool of 171 multiplex PCR primer pairs. The target regions of these primer pairs overlap with the gaps between target regions of the previous pool of 172 primer pairs (Fig. 1B ). Together, these two overlapping pools of primers provide full coverage of the entire viral genome. Most importantly, using both pools in detection would lead to a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability.

options.B: Electrophoresis alone identified SARS-CoV-2 uniquely, making NGS unnecessary
options.C: Defined-size peaks gave a fast indication of a coronavirus-family positive, while NGS identified the specific virus
options.D: Neither was used until after clinical sequencing was complete

questions.rationale: The authors distinguish rapid amplicon-pattern screening from definitive virus identification by sequencing.
questions.evidence_quote: Since dozens of target regions could be amplified from a single copy of SARS-CoV-2, electrophoresis peaks with a defined distribution of peak sizes were expected. Multiplex PCR could potentially amplify not only SARS-CoV-2, but also other coronaviruses, due to shared sequence similarities despite the fact that we designed primers specific to the SARS-CoV-2 genome to avoid cross amplification. In that context, electrophoresis analysis provides a fast and sensitive indication of infection from at least that family of viruses. For specificity, the generated NGS sequencing library can be interrogated for definitive identification of the specific virus.
